title: Practicing dying
hookLine: in the Phaedo, Socrates calls philosophy a practice of dying, and his friend laughs

lines: A CELL ON THE LAST DAY.
cards: A prison cell in Athens, on the last day. Socrates's friends have come early. His wife and small son have been with him and been sent home.
The talk turns to philosophy, and Socrates says something so strange that his friend Simmias laughs out loud: people who do philosophy rightly are doing nothing other than practicing dying.
The crowd would agree, Simmias says, still laughing: philosophers do seem half dead already. Socrates doesn't mind the joke. He means something else.

teach.h: THOSE WHO LOVE WISDOM PRACTICE DYING.
teach.b: First, the claim. In Plato's dialogue the Phaedo, Socrates says those who truly love wisdom are practicing dying and being dead, so of all people they should be least afraid when death actually comes.
Someone who trains all their life for something shouldn't panic when it arrives. Second, what he means by dying.
For Plato's Socrates, death is the soul's release from the body, and philosophy is a rehearsal of that release.

teach.h: STEPPING BACK FROM THE BODY'S PULLS.
teach.b: Each time the mind lets go of the body's pulls, hunger and craving, fear and display, the restless wanting more, it steps back from them a little. Philosophy, in his sense, is that stepping back, practiced daily.

This picture rests on a belief: that the soul is separate from the body and can go on without it. Much of the Phaedo argues for that belief. Not everyone in this block shares it; tomorrow's teacher, for one, does not.
That disagreement is real, and it stays standing. Fourth, what can travel. Some readers who don't share Plato's view of the soul still keep the practice.

They hear it as this: every small letting go, a grudge set down, a habit loosened, a possession given away, an argument you don't need to win, is a rehearsal for the larger letting go that comes to everyone.
Practiced small and often, it stops being foreign.

how: Readers of the Phaedo take 'practicing dying' in different ways: as Plato's argument that the soul is freed from the body, or more loosely as a daily habit of small lettings go.

o: fasting until the body is too weak to want
taking needless risks to prove you have no fear
philosophy as a daily rehearsal of letting go

games.q: the Phaedo's idea — tap the pairs.
p: the soul's release from the body

s: Socrates said philosophers should be the least afraid of death
if you've practiced for something all your life, why panic when it comes?
it meant stepping back from the body's pulls: craving, fear, wanting more.
the idea rests on Plato's belief in a soul separate from the body
the Phaedo argues for it, and not every voice in this block agrees.

games.q: you're Socrates's friend in the cell. he says philosophy is practicing dying. what do you do?
o: laugh, and say the crowd would agree.
games.why: Simmias laughs out loud, and Socrates takes the joke in stride and explains what he means.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing you're holding tightly today: a plan that has to go a certain way, a comment you're still chewing on, a phone you keep reaching for.

Notice where the holding sits, a jaw, a hand, a chest, and on each out-breath loosen that spot a little, the way you'd open a fist one finger at a time. You don't have to throw the thing away; just hold it with an open hand.

wordCard.voice: Practicing dying: in Plato's Phaedo, philosophy as a daily rehearsal of letting go, so that the last letting go is not a stranger. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, from the Phaedo: a practice, or rehearsal, of death.

carryVoice: Your line: practice letting go. Simmias laughed, but Socrates meant every word of it. See you tomorrow.
